1.title: you've said it a thousand times
1.hook: you've said it a thousand times — at a table, at a funeral
1.howItsDone: Christians say amen at the end of prayers, hymns and blessings, usually all together, as a way of saying "yes, we agree" to what was just prayed.

segments.voice: You've said this word more times than you could count. At the end of grace, right before anyone's allowed to eat. At a funeral, quietly, along with everyone else. At the end of a song in a church you were only visiting. Maybe as a joke — amen to that. It sounds almost the same from one language to the next, and it's easy to hear it as the end. The prayer's over. You can open your eyes now. It doesn't mean that. It means something closer to the opposite. Today, in a few minutes, you find out what you've been agreeing to.
screen: `AMEN.` → `YOU'VE SAID IT A THOUSAND TIMES.` → `IT DOESN'T MEAN THE END.`

segments.voice: Amen is Hebrew. It comes from a root, aman, that means firm. Solid. The kind of thing you can put your weight on. The same root gives Hebrew its words for faithfulness and for trust. So when someone says amen, they aren't signing off. They're saying: yes. That's solid. I'll stand on that. Truly. So be it. It's old. In the book of Deuteronomy, a list of rules is read out loud to a whole people, and after each one the text says: "And all the people shall answer and say, Amen." A room answering yes. That still happens in church services today. Someone says something, and the room agrees out loud. Then comes a detail that's easy to miss. In the Gospels, Jesus uses the word in a strange place. Not at the end of what he says. At the start. The old King James Bible puts it this way: "Verily, verily, I say unto you." Underneath verily is the same word. Amen, amen. The Gospel of John has him say it like that again and again. Usually amen came after, to agree with something already said. He said it first, like a man vouching for his words before he spoke them. And the last book of the Bible goes one step further. It calls him "the Amen, the faithful and true witness." Not just someone who says yes. The yes itself.
screen: `AMEN — FIRM. SOLID.` · `NOT GOODBYE. YES.` · `THE ROOM ANSWERS.` · `HE SAID IT FIRST.` · then, large: `THE YES AT THE END OF A PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice for day one, and it's small on purpose. One breath, with the bell. Breathe in slowly, all the way. And on the way out, if you want to, say the word, out loud or just in your head. Amen. Not to end anything. To agree with something. You're here. You showed up. That's worth a yes.
Amen. Truly. So be it. The word you've said your whole life, and now you know it's a yes, not a goodbye. First word on your strand.
screen: `AMEN — your 1st word` → clicks onto an empty word-strand.

segments.voice: Your line to carry: let it be so. Once today, when someone says something true — a friend, a stranger, a song — notice it, and say yes to it inside. That's day one. You showed up. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A GIFT YOU DIDN'T EARN.`

2.title: a gift you didn't earn
2.hook: a gift you didn't earn; your grandmother said it before dinner
2.tomorrow: a carpenter's son from a nowhere town
2.howItsDone: Many Christians say grace, a short prayer of thanks, before meals, and churches speak of grace as God's free gift, received in faith and, for many, through sacraments like baptism and communion.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was amen, and your line was let it be so. Did you catch yourself saying yes to something true? Hold on to that yes. Day two.

The food is on the kitchen table, everybody's hungry, and somebody's grandmother says: wait. We haven't said grace. Heads go down. A few words, maybe the same words she's said every night for fifty years. Then amen, and the forks move. If you grew up with that, saying grace probably meant saying thanks. And it does. But grace is a much bigger word than a mealtime prayer. Christians use it for something much larger. It means a gift you didn't earn. Once you hear it that way, it starts turning up everywhere.
screen: `WE HAVEN'T SAID GRACE.` → `NOT JUST THANKS.` → `A GIFT YOU DIDN'T EARN.`

segments.voice: The Greek word in the New Testament is charis. It means a gift, a favor, kindness given freely. It's where English gets charisma: a gift someone just has. And it hides inside another church word, Eucharist, which means thanksgiving. In Greek, the gift and the thank-you belong to one word family. Now the part that cuts against the grain. So much of life runs on earning. You work, you get paid. You study, you pass. Grace doesn't work like that. The letter to the Ephesians says it plainly: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." Not of yourselves. Not a wage. A gift. Paul, writing to the Corinthians, describes a problem he begged the Lord three times to take away. He never says what it was. The answer he says he got was this: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." Not the problem removed. Enough, given, right inside it. Churches have long argued about how grace reaches a person: through the sacraments, like baptism and communion, through faith, through both. But the word itself keeps its meaning: given, not earned. Christians draw a hope from that: nobody is too far behind for it. The grandmother at the table wasn't paying for dinner. She was saying: this came to us. We didn't make all of it. Thank you.
screen: `CHARIS — A GIFT, FREELY GIVEN.` · `IN GREEK, GIFT AND THANKS ARE KIN.` · `NOT OF YOURSELVES.` · `ENOUGH, INSIDE THE PROBLEM.` · then, large: `GIVEN, NOT EARNED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice for day two. One breath, with the bell. Before you take it, notice this: you didn't make this breath. It just came. Your lungs have been doing it all day while you weren't paying attention. So breathe in slowly, and let it be a gift you didn't earn. And on the way out, if you want to, say thank you, out loud or inside. That's all grace is at a dinner table.
Grace. A gift you didn't earn, from the Greek charis. Second word on your strand.

Your line to carry: you are already held. Once today, notice something good you didn't earn. A kindness, a sunset, a stranger holding a door. Don't rush to pay it back. Just receive it. That's day two.

screen: `DAY 2 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A CARPENTER'S SON FROM A NOWHERE TOWN.`

3.title: a carpenter's son from a nowhere town, not a stained-glass window
3.hook: a carpenter's son from a nowhere town, not a stained-glass window
3.carry: he ate with the wrong people on purpose
3.howItsDone: Christians come to know Jesus mainly through the four Gospels, read aloud in church services, and they pray to him or in his name.

segments.voice: Two words in. Amen, a yes. Grace, a gift you didn't earn. Your line was: you are already held. Did you pause before a meal? Day three.

A stained-glass window, lit from behind. A painting with a golden circle around his head. A calm face on a card in a hospital waiting room. Those are the usual pictures of Jesus. Now try this instead. A man with rough hands. Sawdust, or stone dust, on his clothes. A family the neighbors knew by name: his mother, his brothers, his sisters. When he started to teach, the neighbors weren't impressed. They were confused. Isn't that just the builder? Christians believe a great deal about who he was. But the Gospels start somewhere very ordinary, and so does today.
screen: `NOT A STAINED-GLASS WINDOW.` → `ROUGH HANDS. A KNOWN FAMILY.` → `ISN'T THAT JUST THE BUILDER?`

segments.voice: Start with the name. Jesus is the English form of a Greek name, which comes from the Hebrew Yeshua, the same name as Joshua. It means, roughly, God saves, and Matthew's Gospel ties the name to saving. It wasn't a rare name: the letter to the Colossians mentions another man called Jesus. Then the job. When he comes home and teaches, Mark's Gospel has the neighbors ask, in the King James words: "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?" Matthew has it: "Is not this the carpenter's son?" The Greek word is tekton. A builder, a craftsman. It could mean wood, and it could mean stone. Either way: a working man with a trade. Then the town. Nazareth, in Galilee, a place nobody in the story expects much from. When a man named Nathanael first hears where Jesus is from, he says: "Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?" And his friend Philip answers with three words: "Come and see." In Mark, though, what gets people talking isn't where he came from. It's who he sits down with. He eats at the house of a tax collector named Levi, at a table full of people others avoided. Some religious teachers watching ask his followers how he can eat with tax collectors and sinners. He hears, and answers: healthy people don't need a doctor. Sick people do. In the story, the meal itself is the message. He shared the table with the wrong people, and he did it on purpose. Christians say much more about Jesus: that he is the Son of God, that he died and rose again. The path gets to all of that. It starts at a table.
screen: `YESHUA — THE NAME JOSHUA.` · `TEKTON — A BUILDER.` · `NAZARETH — COME AND SEE.` · `A TABLE WITH THE WRONG PEOPLE.` · then, large: `IT STARTS AT A TABLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Three breaths, with the bell. On the first, picture a table. Any table you've eaten at. On the second, notice who is usually sitting at it. On the third, picture one person who usually isn't. Someone you'd never think to invite. Just give them a chair, in your mind, for one breath. If you pray, you can bring them with you into it.
Jesus. Yeshua. A builder's name from a small town, the name at the center of the whole Christian path. Third word.
Your line: he ate with the wrong people on purpose. Today, if you can, sit with someone you usually wouldn't. At lunch, on a call, for five minutes. That's day three.

4.title: "our father"
4.hook: "Our Father" — the word he chose was the family one
4.howItsDone: Christians pray the Lord's Prayer at home and in church, where the congregation often says it together, aloud.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Jesus, the carpenter's son who ate with the wrong people on purpose. Did you pull out a chair for anyone? Today we start the prayer he taught. Day four.

Weddings, funerals, school assemblies, a locker room before a big game. Our Father, who art in heaven. You may have heard a room full of people say it together without anyone holding a page. Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Christians all pray it. For the next five days, we'll go through it one line at a time, from the first words to the last. Today, just the opening. Because the way you start talking to someone tells you who you think they are. And Jesus started with a family word.
screen: `A PRAYER SAID BY HEART.` → `FIVE DAYS, ONE LINE A DAY.` → `IT STARTS WITH A FAMILY WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the opening, as the King James Bible gives it in Matthew chapter six: "Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name." Start with father. The Gospels were written in Greek, and the word there is pater. But Jesus spoke Aramaic, and once, in Mark, the Gospel keeps his own word. In Gethsemane, the night before he died, he prays: "Abba, Father, all things are possible unto thee." Abba is the family word. What a child says at home, and what a grown son still says to his dad. You may have heard it means daddy. Scholars have pushed back on that: grown children used it too, so it isn't baby talk. But it isn't a courtroom title either. It's the word you'd use at home. And Paul, writing to the Romans, puts it in the mouths of believers: "whereby we cry, Abba, Father." Now the other word. Our. Not my. The whole prayer never once says I, me or my. It's our, us, our, us, all the way through. Even said alone in a quiet room, the prayer assumes a family around you. Then hallowed: an old English word for holy. May your name be treated as holy. So the first line holds two things at once. Close enough to call him father. Still holy. That's line one of five.
screen: `PATER, ABBA — FATHER.` · `ABBA — THE KITCHEN-TABLE WORD.` · `OUR, NOT MY.` · `HALLOWED — HOLY.` · then, large: `CLOSE, AND STILL HOLY.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, think of the word our, and let one person you love come to mind. On the second, widen it to the people you'll pass today, strangers included. On the third, if you pray, you can say the line: Our Father, which art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. If you don't, just rest in the word our, and the people it takes in.
Line one of the Lord's Prayer. Our Father: the family word, with a family around you. Fourth on your strand.
Your line to carry: you're not addressing a stranger. Today, when you talk to someone you love, use the name only you call them. Notice what that one word does. That's day four.

5.title: "thy kingdom come"
5.hook: "thy kingdom come" — not a place, a way things could be
5.howItsDone: Christians pray "thy kingdom come" each time they say the Lord's Prayer, and many describe God's kingdom as already begun in Jesus and not yet complete.

segments.voice: Yesterday, line one of the Lord's Prayer: Our Father. The family word, and our, not my. Did you catch yourself saying someone's name a little differently? Now, line two. Day five.

Say the word kingdom and you probably see a place. Castles on a map. Borders. A throne in some far-off city. So when people pray thy kingdom come, it can sound like asking for a place to arrive at, someday, somewhere up there. But look at what the prayer says right after those three words. It doesn't point up. It points down, to here. We're on line two of five, and it may be the most hopeful line in the whole prayer.
screen: `KINGDOM — A PLACE ON A MAP?` → `IT POINTS DOWN, TO HERE.`

segments.voice: Here it is, from Matthew: "Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven." The Greek word for kingdom is basileia, and it means less a territory than a reign. Not where a king lives. How things go when he's in charge. So thy kingdom come is closer to: let your way of running things happen. And then it says where. In earth, as it is in heaven. Not us going up. The way things are there, coming down here. Jesus talked about this kingdom more than almost anything else. Mark sums up his first preaching with a line that includes: "the kingdom of God is at hand." At hand. Near. Within reach. In Luke he says, "the kingdom of God is within you," and here's an honest puzzle: the Greek can mean within you, or among you, right in your midst. Translators still argue. So is it now, or later? Christians have held both for two thousand years. Many put it this way: already, and not yet. Already, whenever someone is fed, healed or forgiven. Not yet, because look around. And the pictures Jesus used for it are small on purpose: a mustard seed, a little yeast worked into dough. Something huge, starting tiny. So when someone prays this line, they aren't only asking for a someday. They're asking for a today.
screen: `BASILEIA — A REIGN, NOT A PLACE.` · `IN EARTH, AS IT IS IN HEAVEN.` · `AT HAND. WITHIN YOU. AMONG YOU.` · `ALREADY, AND NOT YET.` · then, large: `A SEED, A LITTLE YEAST.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, think of one place in your life that isn't how it should be. A room, a friendship, a street. On the second, picture it the way it could be. Just a little better. On the third, if you pray, you can say the line: thy kingdom come, thy will be done. If you don't, simply hold that picture for a breath: the way things could be, right there.
Line two of the Lord's Prayer. Thy kingdom come: not a place far away, a way things could be, here. Fifth on your strand.
Your line to carry: here, now, would be fine. Today, do one small thing that makes a corner of the world a little more the way it should be. Pick up the litter. Send the kind text. That's day five.

6.title: "daily bread"
6.hook: "daily bread" — just today's; the prayer that refuses to hoard
6.howItsDone: Christians pray "give us this day our daily bread" each time they say the Lord's Prayer. Catholic and Orthodox Christians often connect the line with the bread of communion as well as ordinary food.

segments.voice: Yesterday, line two of the Lord's Prayer: thy kingdom come. Not a place far off, a way things could be, here. Your line was here, now, would be fine. Did you make one corner a little better? Now, line three. Day six.

Open a pantry, a fridge, or the notes app where the plans live, and there's usually some stocking up going on. The extra pack of pasta. The backup charger. The savings account checked at 2am. It makes sense. Tomorrow is uncertain, and a full shelf can feel like safety. Now here's the middle of the Lord's Prayer. After the Father and the kingdom, the prayer finally asks for something for us. And what it asks for is small. Not a full shelf. Not the year sorted. Just bread. Just today's. We're on line three of five, and it's the line that refuses to hoard.
screen: `THE SHELF WE KEEP STOCKING.` → `THE PRAYER FINALLY ASKS FOR US.` → `JUST TODAY'S.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, from Matthew: "Give us this day our daily bread." Bread, in that world, meant food, the thing you actually ate to stay alive. So this is the plainest request in the prayer. And it has an old story behind it. In Exodus, the people of Israel are in the desert, hungry, and every morning something to eat lies on the ground. They call it manna. The rule is simple: gather what you need for today. Some people gather extra and keep it overnight, and by morning it has spoiled. The Bible puts the result this way: "he that gathered much had nothing over, and he that gathered little had no lack." Enough for everyone. Nothing to stockpile. It comes from the scripture Jesus and his first listeners shared. Now an honest puzzle. The Greek word translated daily is epiousios. An early Christian writer, Origen, said he couldn't find it anywhere else in Greek, and thought the Gospel writers may have coined it. It might mean for today. It might mean for tomorrow. It might mean what we need to exist. Jerome, translating the Bible into Latin, used two different words for it in two different Gospels. Nobody knows for sure. Churches hear it in different ways, too. Catholic and Orthodox Christians often hear in daily bread both ordinary food and the bread of communion. Many Protestants hear first the plain food on the table, and some add the word of God. Whatever epiousios means, one word in the line is plain: us. Give us. Not give me. Enough for today, for everyone at the table.
screen: `BREAD — THE PLAINEST REQUEST.` · `MANNA: GATHER ONLY TODAY'S.` · `EPIOUSIOS — NOBODY IS SURE.` · then, large: `GIVE US, NOT GIVE ME.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, think of what you'll eat today. Just today. On the second, notice one thing you're worried won't be enough tomorrow, and set it down for one breath. On the third, if you pray, you can say the line: give us this day our daily bread. If you don't, simply notice: for today, there is enough.
Line three of the Lord's Prayer. Give us this day our daily bread: a small request, for today, for all of us. Sixth word.
Your line to carry: enough for today. Before you buy one more thing today, pause and ask: is there enough already? And if there's extra, share it. Day six.

7.title: "forgive us as we forgive"
7.hook: "forgive us as we forgive" — the one clause with a condition in it
7.howItsDone: Christians pray this line every time they say the Lord's Prayer. Some churches say "debts," others "trespasses," from the Book of Common Prayer, and some use Luke's "sins."

segments.voice: Yesterday, line three: give us this day our daily bread. Just today's, and for all of us. Your line was enough for today. Did you notice when there already was enough? Now, line four. Day seven.

Read the fine print. Contracts have it: the little clause that says, this only works if. Now look at the Lord's Prayer. Its lines are plain requests. Your kingdom come. Give us bread. Deliver us. But one line has a condition built right into it, and it's the line we're on today. Forgive us, as we forgive. It's a strange thing to pray, if you stop and listen. It asks to be forgiven the same way we forgive other people. Which means the person who cut you off, the friend who never paid you back, the sibling who said the thing, all of them just walked into the prayer. Line four of five.
screen: `THE FINE PRINT.` → `ONE LINE WITH A CONDITION.` → `EVERYONE WHO OWES YOU, INSIDE.`

segments.voice: In the old King James Bible, Matthew chapter six, it reads: "And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors." Debts. Money language. Jesus spoke Aramaic, and scholars point out that in Aramaic one word could mean a debt or a sin: something you owe. So forgiving is like tearing up an IOU. Not collecting. Churches today say the line in different words. Some say debts. Others say trespasses, the word in the old Book of Common Prayer: "forgive us our trespasses." Luke's version says sins. Same idea, three doors into it. Now the Greek verb for forgive. It's aphiemi, and its first meaning is to let go. To release. To send away, the way you'd open your hand and let a bird fly off. Forgiving, in this word, isn't pretending it didn't happen, and Christian teachers often add that it isn't the same as trusting someone again. It's letting go of the debt. Then a detail in Matthew. When Jesus finishes teaching the prayer in Matthew, he goes back and comments on only one line. This one. "For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you." Out of the whole prayer, that's the part he underlines. Christians have wrestled with it ever since. One long-standing reading: God's forgiveness is a gift, never a wage, and a forgiven person becomes someone who forgives. Read any way, the two go together. You can't hold your hand open to receive and keep it clenched at the same time. And this is day seven, the end of a week. Amen, grace, Jesus, our Father, the kingdom, bread, and now: let it go.
screen: `DEBTS — TEARING UP THE IOU.` · `APHIEMI — TO LET GO.` · `THE ONE LINE HE UNDERLINES.` · then, large: `AN OPEN HAND.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, make a fist, and think of one small thing someone owes you. Not the biggest wound. Something small. On the second, keep holding it, and notice how tight that feels. On the third, open your hand as you breathe out. If you pray, you can say the line: forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.
